entities.name: Aesop's Fables
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Aesop's Fables are a collection of didactic stories attributed to Aesop — a semi-legendary Greek slave and storyteller said to have lived in ancient Greece c. 620–564 BCE — that use animals as characters to convey moral lessons. Transmitted orally for centuries and later collected in various written compilations, the fables have been among the most widely read and influential texts in world literature, shaping the Western tradition of allegory, moral philosophy, and children's literature.

The historicity of Aesop as an individual is uncertain — ancient sources agree that he was a slave of non-Greek origin (Phrygian, Ethiopian, or Lydian according to different accounts) who won his freedom through his wit. The Life of Aesop, a prose biography compiled in the 1st century CE, presents his biography in largely legendary form. The fables themselves were first collected in written form by Demetrius of Phalerum (c. 320 BCE); Phaedrus (1st century CE) rendered them in Latin verse; Babrius (2nd century CE) in Greek verse. The standard Renaissance collection was made by Heinrich Steinhöwel (1476), printed by Caxton in England (1484).

The most famous fables — the Tortoise and the Hare, the Fox and the Grapes, the Boy Who Cried Wolf, the Crow and the Pitcher — have entered the linguistic fabric of most Western languages as proverbial expressions. Scholars debate the relationship between Aesop's tradition and the Indian Panchatantra/Kalila and Dimna tradition; comparative study suggests shared ancient roots for the fable genre across Eurasian civilizations. Aesop's Fables have been illustrated, retold, and adapted in every century and every culture that has encountered them.
